claim: Microglia represent 5-10% of brain cells in the adult central nervous system (CNS).
source: Microglia represent the largest population of immune cells in the brain, constituting 5–10% of brain cells in the adult central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is a direct statement in the introduction providing a quantitative measure of microglial abundance in the adult CNS.

claim: Microglia are responsible for immune defense and resolution, tissue maintenance, neuronal support, and synaptic integrity.
source: As resident tissue macrophages, microglia are responsible for immune defense and resolution, tissue maintenance, neuronal support, and synaptic integrity (Salter and Stevens, 2017; Tay et al., 2017; Wolf et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Microglia arise from yolk sac-derived erythromyeloid progenitors and colonize the brain as embryonic microglia during early stages of development (E8.5 – E9.5).
source: Microglia arise from yolk sac-derived erythromyeloid progenitors and colonize the brain as embryonic microglia during early stages of development (i.e. E8.5 – E9.5) (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Kierdorf et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: Immature myeloid cells displaying amoeboid morphology and high proliferative potential enter the brain via the meninges and ventricles in mice.
source: These immature myeloid cells, displaying amoeboid morphology and high proliferative potential, enter the brain via the meninges and ventricles in mice (Lelli et al., 2013; Ueno et al., 2013; Swinnen et al., 2013; Xavier et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published studies.

claim: Immature myeloid cells enter the brain via the leptomeninges, choroid plexus, and ventricular zone in humans.
source: as well as, via the leptomeninges, choroid plexus, and ventricular zone in humans (Tay et al., 2017; Verney et al., 2010; Monier et al., 2007; Ginhoux et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published studies.

claim: Microglial colonization occurs first in the white matter (e.g. internal capsule, external capsule, and cerebral peduncle) and continues to the sub- and then cortical plate as cells proliferate and migrate in a radial and tangential manner.
source: Microglial colonization occurs first in the white matter (WM) (e.g. internal capsule, external capsule, and cerebral peduncle) and continues to the sub- and then cortical plate as cells proliferate and migrate in a radial and tangential manner (Verney et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In adulthood (P28 and onward), microglia become fully mature, exhibiting ramified morphology and expressing canonical microglial signature genes: P2ry12, Tmem119, Siglech, Cx3cr1, Olfml3, Fcrls, and Sall1.
source: In adulthood (P28 and onward), microglia become fully mature, exhibiting ramified morphology and expressing canonical microglial signature genes: P2ry12, Tmem119, Siglech, Cx3cr1, Olfml3, Fcrls, and Sall1 (Dubbelaar et al., 2018; Baufeld et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing studies have identified transcriptionally distinct microglial gene signatures associated with disease (e.g. disease-associated microglia [DAM], microglial neurodegenerative [MGnD] phenotype).
source: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing studies have identified transcriptionally distinct microglial gene signatures associated with disease (e.g. disease-associated microglia [DAM], microglial neurodegenerative [MGnD] phenotype [Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Krasemann et al., 2017; Mathys et al., 2017; Masuda et al., 2019])
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published studies.

claim: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing studies have identified transcriptionally distinct microglial gene signatures associated with injury (e.g. injury-responsive microglia [IRM]).
source: injury (e.g. injury-responsive microglia [IRM] Hammond et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing studies have identified transcriptionally distinct microglial gene signatures associated with brain region-specific areas/developmental stages (e.g. proliferative-region-associated microglia [PAM], axon tract-associated microglia [ATM]).
source: and brain region-specific areas/developmental stages (e.g. proliferative-region-associated microglia [PAM], axon tract-associated microglia [ATM] Masuda et al., 2019; Hammond et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published studies.

claim: White matter-associated microglia (WAM) have been identified as a population of microglia in WM tracts from the corpus callosum that share parts of the DAM gene signature, including genes involved in phagocytosis, and increase with aging and disease.
source: including the recent discovery of white matter-associated microglia (WAM) (Safaiyan et al., 2021). WAMs have been identified as a population of microglia in WM tracts from the corpus callosum that share parts of the DAM gene signature, including genes involved in phagocytosis, and increase with aging and disease (Safaiyan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to a published study.

claim: A distinct subset of microglia (PAMs/ATMs) has been described in the axonal tracts of the corpus callosum during development, sharing not only a similar location to WAMs, but morphological (i.e. amoeboid) and phagocytosis-associated gene profile.
source: In line with this, a distinct subset of microglia (PAMs/ATMs) has been described in the axonal tracts of the corpus callosum during development, sharing not only a similar location to WAMs, but morphological (i.e. amoeboid) and phagocytosis-associated gene profile (Masuda et al., 2019; Hammond et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Homeostatic microglia appear less heterogeneous during adulthood.
source: Despite this, homeostatic microglia appear less heterogeneous during adulthood (Hammond et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: Microglial homeostasis and dynamics are maintained by many signaling factors, including transforming growth factor-beta, Il-34, and colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1).
source: Microglial homeostasis and dynamics are maintained by many signaling factors, including transforming growth factor-beta, Il-34, and colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) (Butovsky et al., 2014; Elmore et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: Microglia in the adult brain are long-lived.
source: Recent studies exploring the homeostatic kinetics of the microglia in the adult brain have revealed that these cells are long-lived (Tay et al., 2017; Réu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: Microglia self-renew, even after acute 80–95% depletion and subsequent repopulation.
source: and self-renew, even after acute 80–95% depletion and subsequent repopulation (Elmore et al., 2014; Zhan et al., 2019; Bruttger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: No approach to date has been able to deplete all microglia.
source: However, no approach to date has been able to deplete all microglia (Waisman et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: 7 day treatment of the brain penetrant CSF1R/KIT/FLT3 inhibitor PLX3397 (Pexidartinib; 600 ppm in chow) eliminates ~90–98% of microglia in the CNS.
source: In previous studies, we have shown that 7 day treatment of the brain penetrant CSF1R/KIT/FLT3 inhibitor PLX3397 (Pexidartinib; 600 ppm in chow) eliminates ~90–98% of microglia in the CNS (Elmore et al., 2014; Najafi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: During 7 day PLX3397 depletion, surviving microglia are seen scattered throughout the brain.
source: During depletion, surviving microglia are seen scattered throughout the brain (Figure 1A–B,C)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A-B,C showing scattered surviving microglia.

claim: Subsequent withdrawal of PLX3397 after 7 day treatment results in rapid and spatially homogenous microglial repopulation within 3 days, with cells exceeding control numbers by 7 days.
source: and subsequent withdrawal of the inhibitor results in rapid and spatially homogenous microglial repopulation within 3 days, with cells exceeding control numbers by 7 days (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C,E showing rapid repopulation kinetics.

claim: Repopulation after 7 day PLX3397 treatment is dependent on the local proliferation and clonal expansion of surviving microglia.
source: Recent studies show that repopulation is dependent on the local proliferation and clonal expansion of surviving microglia (Elmore et al., 2014; Zhan et al., 2019; Bruttger et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018; Zhan et al., 2020; Mendes et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to six published studies.

claim: 14 day treatment with PLX3397 (600 ppm) results in pharmacologically unprecedented microglial depletion, in which no IBA1+ cells are observed across whole brain sections.
source: This treatment results in pharmacologically unprecedented microglial depletion, in which we observe no IBA1+ cells across whole brain sections (Figure 1A–B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A-B,D showing absence of IBA1+ cells.

claim: High dose PLX3397 vs. high dose PLX5622 achieves higher CNS exposure and microglial depletion efficiency.
source: Although PLX5622 is a CSF1R inhibitor (CSF1Ri) that is more active against CSF1R compared to other related kinases, studies in our lab have shown that high dose PLX3397 vs. high dose PLX5622 achieves higher CNS exposure and microglial depletion efficiency.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the authors' laboratory comparing two CSF1R inhibitors.

claim: PLX3397 levels remain the same in the CNS despite longer drug exposure (7d vs 14d treatment).
source: Pharmacokinetic analysis of microglia-depleted brains at both 7d and 14d treatment of PLX3397 shows that PLX3397 levels remain the same in the CNS despite longer drug exposure (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1H showing pharmacokinetic data.

claim: At 3 day recovery following 14 day PLX3397 treatment, no IBA1+ cells are detectable in most brain sections.
source: At 3 day recovery following 14 day PLX3397 treatment, no IBA1+ cells are detectable in most brain sections.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: By 7 day recovery following 14 day PLX3397 treatment, IBA1+ cells appear, but are exclusively located near the lateral ventricle and in WM tracts lining the ventricles.
source: By 7 day recovery, IBA1+ cells appear, but are exclusively located near the lateral ventricle and in WM tracts lining the ventricles (Figure 1D2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D2 showing cell location.

claim: By 14 day recovery following 14 day PLX3397 treatment, IBA1+ cells have spread throughout most of the CNS; however, some areas of the cortex (e.g. the piriform cortex) remain unoccupied.
source: By 14 day recovery, IBA1+ cells have spread throughout most of the CNS; however, some areas of the cortex (e.g. the piriform cortex) remain unoccupied (Figure 1D3).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D3 showing cell distribution.

claim: At 14 day recovery following 14 day PLX3397 treatment, areas of the cortex display a distinct 'wave' of cells in adjacent unoccupied cortical areas.
source: These areas display a distinct 'wave' of cells in adjacent unoccupied cortical areas (Figure 1D3).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D3 showing the wave pattern.

claim: At 28 day recovery following 14 day PLX3397 treatment, all brain regions are populated with IBA1+ cells, but absolute cell numbers remain 50% lower compared to microglia in control animals.
source: At 28 day repopulation, all brain regions are populated with IBA1+ cells, but absolute cell numbers remain 50% lower compared to microglia in control animals, as seen in somatosensory cortices (Figure 1D4, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D4, F showing cell quantification.

claim: Within 14–21 days of GLOBAL repopulation, repopulating microglia attain similar densities to resident microglia.
source: We have previously shown that within 14–21 days of GLOBAL repopulation, repopulating microglia not only attain similar densities to resident microglia, but also display similar morphologies, cell surface marker expression, gene expression profiles, and inflammatory responses to LPS (Elmore et al., 2014; Elmore et al., 2015; Elmore et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies by the authors.

claim: WM repopulating cells display larger cell bodies after 7 day recovery (which normalize by 14 day recovery).
source: In contrast, WM repopulating cells display larger cell bodies (Figure 1I–J) after 7 day recovery (which normalize by 14 day recovery)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1I-J showing morphological measurements.

claim: WM repopulating cells display reduced process/filament length compared to homeostatic microglia even after 28 days recovery.
source: as well as reduced process/filament length (Figure 1I,K) and reduced process/dendrite branching and complexity (Figure 1I,L) compared to homeostatic microglia even after 28 days recovery.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1I,K showing morphological measurements.

claim: WM repopulating cells display reduced process/dendrite branching and complexity compared to homeostatic microglia even after 28 days recovery.
source: as well as reduced process/filament length (Figure 1I,K) and reduced process/dendrite branching and complexity (Figure 1I,L) compared to homeostatic microglia even after 28 days recovery.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1I,L showing morphological measurements.

claim: In GLOBAL repopulation, microglia repopulate the brain parenchyma in a homogeneous fashion, with repopulating cells displaying no preference for specific locations.
source: In GLOBAL repopulation, microglia repopulate the brain parenchyma in a homogeneous fashion, with repopulating cells displaying no preference for specific locations (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing spatial distribution.

claim: WM repopulating cells first appear in precise ventricular and WM locations.
source: In contrast, WM repopulating cells first appear in precise ventricular and WM locations (Figure 1D2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D2 showing initial cell locations.

claim: Throughout the rostral-caudal axis, IBA1+ cells initially repopulate the brain within the caudoputamen, particularly in areas near the lateral ventricle and associated WM tracts.
source: Throughout this axis, IBA1+ cells initially repopulate the brain within the caudoputamen, particularly in areas near the lateral ventricle and associated WM tracts.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the spatial heat map analysis.

claim: At rostral regions of the brain, repopulating cells are found within the rostral migratory stream (RMS), a projecting axonal tract from the SVZ to the olfactory bulb.
source: At rostral regions of the brain, cells are found within the rostral migratory stream (RMS), a projecting axonal tract from the SVZ to the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the spatial heat map analysis.

claim: In more caudal brain regions, repopulating cells are seen near the SVZ, caudoputamen, and corpus callosum.
source: In more caudal brain regions, repopulating cells are seen near the SVZ, caudoputamen, and corpus callosum.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the spatial heat map analysis.

claim: Repopulating cells migrate in a radial and tangential fashion, initially filling the WM and caudoputamen before spreading out through the cortex in a dynamic wave between 7 and 14 day recovery.
source: Repopulating cells migrate in a radial and tangential fashion, initially filling the WM and caudoputamen before spreading out through the cortex in a dynamic wave between 7 and 14 day recovery (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B-C showing migration patterns.

claim: At Stage I of WM repopulation, cells are visible near the lateral ventricle at the intersection of the corpus callosum, caudoputmen, and SVZ and appear to migrate in a radial migration pattern from the ventricular zone into and filling the caudoputamen in an inferior direction.
source: At Stage I, cells are visible near the lateral ventricle at the intersection of the corpus callosum, caudoputmen, and SVZ and appear to migrate in a radial migration pattern from the ventricular zone into and filling the caudoputamen in an inferior direction.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis of the migratory wave.

claim: At Stage I of WM repopulation, cells also appear in WM tracts, specifically in the corpus callosum.
source: At this stage, cells also appear in WM tracts, specifically in the corpus callosum.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis of the migratory wave.

claim: At Stage II of WM repopulation, cells begin to migrate in a tangential migration pattern utilizing WM tracts to migrate into WM areas or areas near WM tracts.
source: At Stage II, cells begin to migrate in a tangential migration pattern utilizing WM tracts to migrate into WM areas or areas near WM tracts.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis of the migratory wave.

claim: At Stage III of WM repopulation, repopulating cells continue to migrate in both a radial and tangential migratory pattern filling ~80–95% of the striatum, including the caudoputamen, lateral septal complex, and pallidum.
source: At Stage III, repopulating cells continue to migrate in both a radial and tangential migratory pattern filling ~80–95% of the striatum, including the caudoputamen, lateral septal complex, and pallidum.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis of the migratory wave.

claim: At Stage III of WM repopulation, repopulating cells are restricted or unable to migrate past the WM tract or corpus callosum between the cerebral nuclei and cerebral cortex.
source: It is also apparent that repopulating cells are restricted or unable to migrate past the WM tract or corpus callosum between the cerebral nuclei and cerebral cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1B showing migration restriction.

claim: At Stage IV of WM repopulation, the cells have broken through the WM tract barrier and migrate out in a radial migration pattern moving from the subcortical to the cortical plate.
source: At Stage IV, the cells have broken through this WM tract barrier and migrate out in a radial migration pattern moving from the subcortical to the cortical plate (Figure 2B–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B showing migration patterns.

claim: Proliferating WM repopulating myeloid cells are initially found near ventricles and WM tracts.
source: In contrast to the proliferative profile of previously described GLOBAL-repopulating microglia, in which remaining microglia proliferate throughout the brain to give rise to newly repopulating cells, proliferating WM repopulating myeloid cells are initially found near ventricles and WM tracts (Figure 2E and E1, Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E, E1, F-G showing proliferation patterns.

claim: As WM repopulating cells spread and migrate through the brain, proliferation remains localized within the cell 'wavefront'.
source: As the cells spread and migrate through the brain, proliferation remains localized within the cell 'wavefront' (Figure 2F, F and F4).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2F, F4 showing proliferation localization.

claim: Once out of the wavefront (i.e. in the wake of the wave) IBA1+ cells appear to stop proliferating (i.e. Ki67-).
source: Once out of the front (i.e. in the wake of the wave) IBA1+ cells appear to stop proliferating (i.e. Ki67-; Figure 2F3).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2F3 showing lack of proliferation marker.

claim: The wave of proliferating cells is most apparent at Stage IV, led by a wavefront with an average width of ~100–150 µm of amoeboid and proliferating myeloid cells.
source: This wave of proliferating cells is most apparent at Stage IV, led by a wavefront with an average width of ~100–150 µm of amoeboid and proliferating myeloid cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the analysis of the migratory wave.

claim: Following 14 day PLX3397 treatment, a very small number of surviving IBA1+ cells (~15 in 14 day treated PLX3397 brains vs. ~132,000 in control brains = 99.98% depletion) are observed exclusively in ventricular (i.e. SVZ) and adjacent WM areas.
source: With this extensive analysis, we observe a very small number of surviving IBA1+ cells in treated brains (~15 in 14 day treated PLX3397 brains vs. ~132,000 in control brains = 99.98% depletion; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). Despite this, we describe the highest reported loss of microglial cells in the adult brain. Notably, these few cells (0.02% of cells) are seen exclusively in ventricular (i.e. SVZ) and adjacent WM areas (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Figure 3A-D showing cell quantification and location.

claim: Surviving SVZ/WM cells following 14 day PLX3397 treatment display a lack of canonical microglial markers, including P2RY12 and TMEM119, as well as distinct morphological profiles.
source: These cells display a lack of canonical microglial markers, including P2RY12 and TMEM119, as well as distinct morphological profiles (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3E-G showing marker expression and morphology.

claim: Examination of brains depleted for 3.5 month PLX3397 (600 ppm) revealed no further surviving cells in the WM/WVZ, suggesting that these cells eventually succumb to CSF1Ri.
source: Examination of brains depleted for 3.5 month PLX3397 (600 ppm) revealed no further surviving cells in the WM/WVZ, suggesting that these cells eventually succumb to CSF1Ri (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H showing absence of cells after prolonged treatment.

claim: The population of microglia residing in the adult SVZ and adjacent RMS display a distinct morphological profile with an amoeboid cell body and fewer/shorter branched processes and exhibit an activated phenotype, similar to WM repopulating cells.
source: Reports show that the population of microglia residing in the adult SVZ and adjacent RMS display a distinct morphological profile with an amoeboid cell body and fewer/shorter branched processes and exhibit an activated phenotype, similar to WM repopulating cells (Ribeiro Xavier et al., 2015; Goings et al., 2006; Böttcher et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Prior descriptions of myeloid cells found in the adult SVZ have found lower expression levels of the microglial-specific marker P2RY12.
source: Prior descriptions of myeloid cells found in the adult SVZ have found lower expression levels of the microglial-specific marker P2RY12 (Ribeiro Xavier et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Repopulating cells are initially negative for both microglial-specific P2RY12 and TMEM119 surface markers, however, express these markers by 28 day recovery.
source: Here, we find repopulating cells are initially negative for both microglial-specific P2RY12 and TMEM119 surface markers, however, express these markers by 28 day recovery (Figure 3H–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3H-I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E showing marker expression over time.

claim: Comparing 14 day PLX3397-treated brains to 7 day recovery brains revealed that the most upregulated genes in the 7 day recovery brain are involved in myeloid cell activation/priming, pathogen sensing, and monocyte-macrophage signaling (e.g. Mrc1, C3ar1, Ccl12, Clec7a, Ccr2/Ccl2, Cybb, and Ccl9), rather than homeostatic microglia signature genes.
source: Comparing 14 day PLX3397-treated brains (i.e. microglial-depleted) to 7 day recovery brains allowed us to explore the gene expression profile of the initial repopulating cells. This comparison revealed that the most upregulated genes in the 7 day recovery brain are involved in myeloid cell activation/priming, pathogen sensing, and monocyte-macrophage signaling (e.g. Mrc1, C3ar1, Ccl12, Clec7a, Ccr2/Ccl2, Cybb, and Ccl9), rather than homeostatic microglia signature genes (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3K showing gene expression analysis.

claim: In comparing 28 day recovery brains to controls, increased expression was detected in several genes associated with myeloid cell signaling (Ccl8, Cmah, Ly9, Lyz2, Tlr8, C4b), in particular, major histocompatibility complex I (H2-D1) and II (H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, Cd74) components and microglial priming (Clec7a, Cybb).
source: In comparing 28 day recovery brains to controls, increased expression was detected in several genes associated with myeloid cell signaling (Ccl8, Cmah, Ly9, Lyz2, Tlr8, C4b), in particular, major histocompatibility complex I (H2-D1) and II (H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, Cd74) components and microglial priming (Clec7a, Cybb) (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3L showing gene expression analysis.

claim: WM repopulated cells are susceptible to CSF1Ri treatment and require CSF1R signaling for their survival once migrated from the SVZ.
source: At both recovery times, the majority of cells were eliminated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K) showing that WM repopulated cells are susceptible to CSF1Ri treatment and require CSF1R signaling for their survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1K showing cell elimination after re-treatment.

claim: H2K-BCL2 mice display elevated microglial densities.
source: Similar to reports in Vav-Bcl2 mice (Askew et al., 2017), these mice display elevated microglial densities (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A showing microglial quantification and a citation to a published study.

claim: In H2K-BCL2 mice, 14 day treatment with PLX3397 (600 ppm) leads to a 61–95% elimination of microglia.
source: In H2K-BCL2 mice, 14 day treatment with PLX3397 (600 ppm) leads to a 61–95% elimination of microglia (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B-D showing microglial depletion in BCL2 mice.

claim: Overexpression of BCL2 in myeloid cells affords some resistance to tissue macrophage loss in Osteopetrotic (op/op) mice, a mouse lacking functional CSF1.
source: In line with this, a previous study has shown that overexpression of BCL2 in myeloid cells affords some resistance to tissue macrophage loss in Osteopetrotic (op/op) mice, a mouse lacking functional CSF1 (Lagasse and Weissman, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: BCL2 is a major regulator of apoptosis, and enhanced Bcl2 expression promotes the survival of cells of myeloid cells.
source: BCL2 is a major regulator of apoptosis, and enhanced Bcl2 expression promotes the survival of cells of myeloid cells (Ogilvy et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: CSF1Ri-induced microglial cell death is caspase-dependent.
source: We and others have shown that CSF1Ri-induced microglial cell death is caspase-dependent (Elmore et al., 2014; Hagan et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: Subsequent withdrawal of CSF1Ri from H2K-BCL2 mice elicits GLOBAL repopulation, rather than WM repopulation, indicating that WM repopulation occurs due to the unprecedented level of microglia depletion rather than drug treatment.
source: Importantly, subsequent withdrawal of CSF1Ri elicits GLOBAL repopulation, rather than WM repopulation (Figure 4B–D), indicating that WM repopulation occurs due to the unprecedented level of microglia depletion rather than drug treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4B-D showing repopulation pattern in BCL2 mice.

claim: Between 3 and 5 day recovery, repopulating cells transiently express NESTIN (92% of IBA1 cells were NESTIN+ at 5 day recovery).
source: Between 3 and 5 day recovery, repopulating cells transiently express NESTIN (92% of IBA1 cells were NESTIN+ at 5 day recovery; Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F showing marker expression.

claim: Between 3 and 5 day recovery, repopulating cells transiently express MASH1 (81% of IBA1 cells were MASH1+ at 5 day recovery).
source: MASH1 (81% of IBA1 cells were MASH1+ at 5 day recovery; Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G showing marker expression.

claim: Between 3 and 5 day recovery, repopulating cells transiently express TIE2 (50% of IBA1 cells were TIE2+ at 5 day recovery).
source: and TIE2 (50% of IBA1 cells were TIE2+ at 5 day recovery; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,H)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,H showing marker expression.

claim: Repopulating cells are negative for GFAP (0% of IBA1 cells were GFAP+ at any timepoint during recovery).
source: but are negative for GFAP (0% of IBA1 cells were GFAP+ at any timepoint during recovery; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing lack of marker expression.

claim: Repopulating cells are negative for DCX (0% of IBA1 cells were DCX+ during recovery).
source: DCX (0% of IBA1 cells were DCX+ during recovery; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing lack of marker expression.

claim: Repopulating cells are negative for OLIG2 (0% of IBA1 cells were OLIG2+ during recovery).
source: OLIG2 (0% of IBA1 cells were OLIG2+ during recovery; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing lack of marker expression.

claim: Repopulating cells are negative for SOX2 (0% of IBA1 cells were SOX2+ during recovery).
source: and SOX2 (0% of IBA1 cells were SOX2+ during recovery; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) at all timepoints.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1E showing lack of marker expression.

claim: Repopulating cells do not originate from Ascl1+ (0% of IBA1 cells were YFP+ during recovery) cell sources.
source: These studies revealed that repopulating cells do not originate from Ascl1+ (0% of IBA1 cells were YFP+ during recovery; Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5C showing lineage tracing results.

claim: Repopulating cells do not originate from Nestin+ (0% of IBA1 cells were YFP+ during recovery) cell sources.
source: or Nestin+ (0% of IBA1 cells were YFP+ during recovery; Figure 5D) cell sources, despite their transient expression of these markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5D showing lineage tracing results.

claim: The Cre-recombinase from the Cx3cr1CreERT2 line is leaky in the absence of tamoxifen (8% of microglia express YFP in control brains and 12% of microglia express YFP during at 7 day recovery).
source: Consistent with previous reports (Fonseca et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2019), we found that the Cre-recombinase from the Cx3cr1CreERT2 line is leaky in the absence of tamoxifen (8% of microglia express YFP in control brains and 12% of microglia express YFP during at 7 day recovery; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-D showing leaky expression and citations to two published studies.

claim: 94% of microglia in control brains expressed YFP in Cx3cr1CreERT2 mice.
source: Despite this, we show that 94% of microglia in control brains expressed YFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,B showing lineage tracing quantification.

claim: 100% of surviving microglia expressed YFP following 14 days of PLX3397 in Cx3cr1CreERT2 mice.
source: 100% of surviving microglia expressed YFP following 14 days of PLX3397 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,B showing lineage tracing quantification.

claim: 95% of repopulating microglial cells expressed YFP at 7 day recovery in Cx3cr1CreERT2 mice, thereby demonstrating that the majority of repopulating cells derive from a Cx3cr1+ cell source.
source: and 95% of repopulating microglial cells expressed YFP at 7 day recovery (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), thereby demonstrating that the majority of repopulating cells derive from a Cx3cr1+ cell source (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and Figure 5E showing lineage tracing quantification.

claim: Repopulating cells initially appear between 3 and 7 days recovery, with IBA1+/Ki67+ cells apparent within the SVZ and the adjacent caudoputamen by 7 days recovery.
source: Immunohistochemical analyses for IBA1 and Ki67 show that repopulating cells initially appear between 3 and 7 days recovery, with IBA1+/Ki67+ cells apparent within the SVZ and the adjacent caudoputamen by 7 days recovery (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5F showing immunohistochemical staining.

claim: Repopulating cells first populate the parenchyma in the SVZ, specifically from a Ki67+-dense region located along the alpha arm of the SVZ (αSVZ) and posterior RMS (pRMS).
source: Further evaluation of sagittal sections from mice at 5 day recovery confirms that repopulating cells first populate the parenchyma in the SVZ, specifically from a Ki67+-dense region located along the alpha arm of the SVZ (αSVZ) and posterior RMS (pRMS) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5G showing cell location and proliferation.

claim: Repopulating cells subsequently accumulate in the WM areas adjacent to the SVZ (i.e. the corpus callosum), caudoputamen, RMS, olfactory bulb, internal capsule, and cerebral peduncle before eventually filling the parenchymal grey matter.
source: These cells subsequently accumulate in the WM areas adjacent to the SVZ (i.e. the corpus callosum), caudoputamen, RMS, olfactory bulb, internal capsule, and cerebral peduncle before eventually filling the parenchymal grey matter (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 5H showing cell distribution.

claim: The internal capsule connects the cerebral peduncle, caudoputamen, and RMS, while the RMS connects the SVZ to the olfactory bulb, providing anatomical pathways by which repopulating cells travel to specific brain locations.
source: The internal capsule connects the cerebral peduncle, caudoputamen, and RMS, while the RMS connects the SVZ to the olfactory bulb, providing anatomical pathways by which repopulating cells travel to specific brain locations.
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity based on known neuroanatomy.

claim: The niches where repopulating cells initially appear are the precise locations in which microglia initially colonize the developing brain.
source: Of note, the aforementioned niches are the precise locations in which microglia initially colonize the developing brain (Ueno et al., 2013; Verney et al., 2010; Ginhoux et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: During the 14th – 17th week of gestation in the developing human brain, microglia are found near or within: the optic tract, the WM junction between the thalamus and internal capsule, and the junction between the internal capsule and the cerebral peduncle.
source: During the 14th – 17th week of gestation in the developing human brain, microglia are found near or within: the optic tract, the WM junction between the thalamus and internal capsule, and the junction between the internal capsule and the cerebral peduncle (Menassa and Gomez-Nicola, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: A second population of amoeboid CX3CR1-expressing microglia emerge from the ventricular zone at embryonic day 20 (E20) and infiltrate the corpus callosum during post-natal day 3–7 (P3-P7).
source: Furthermore, a recent study has shown that a second population of amoeboid CX3CR1-expressing microglia emerge from the ventricular zone at embryonic day 20 (E20) and infiltrate the corpus callosum during post-natal day 3–7 (P3-P7) (Nemes-Baran et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: 227 DEGs were identified (FDR < 0.05) between control and 5 day recovery SVZ tissue.
source: In comparing control vs. 5 day recovery, 227 DEGs were identified (FDR < 0.05) between the two groups (Figure 6B)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 6B showing differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The majority of DEGs between control and 5 day recovery SVZ tissue are downregulated microglia-enriched/related genes, reflecting the reduced pool of myeloid cells in the CNS during the early stages of repopulation.
source: with the majority being downregulated microglia-enriched/related genes, reflecting the reduced pool of myeloid cells in the CNS during the early stages of repopulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential gene expression data.

claim: Upregulated non-myeloid enriched DEGs in depleted vs. 5 day recovery SVZ tissue consisted of genes implicated in cell cycle regulation (Pak3, Swi5, Psmd11, Stat3), DNA transcription/recombination/repair/expression (Alyref2, Swi5, Zfp612, Zfp51, Thumpd1, Prmt5, Taok3, Psmd11, Tox, Stat3), cell adhesion/migration/proliferation (Pak3, Anxa1, Cadm1) and development (Gfap, Rab14, Zfp612).
source: Upregulated non-myeloid enriched DEGs in depleted vs. 5 day recovery mice (Figure 6B) consisted of genes implicated in cell cycle regulation (Pak3, Swi5, Psmd11, Stat3), DNA transcription/recombination/repair/expression (Alyref2, Swi5, Zfp612, Zfp51, Thumpd1, Prmt5, Taok3, Psmd11, Tox, Stat3), cell adhesion/migration/proliferation (Pak3, Anxa1, Cadm1) and development (Gfap, Rab14, Zfp612).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 6B showing differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of DEGs between control and 5d recovery SVZ tissue identified the following top four enriched pathways: myeloid cell differentiation, leukocyte immunity, leukocyte activation, leukocyte chemotaxis and phagocytosis.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of DEGs between control and 5d recovery SVZ tissue identified the following top four enriched pathways: myeloid cell differentiation, leukocyte immunity, leukocyte activation, leukocyte chemotaxis and phagocytosis (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 6C showing GO analysis results.

claim: P2ry12, Siglech, Trem2, Cd33 and Cx3cr1 were least enriched during initial repopulation, whereas Ccl12, Cd52, Lyz2, Itgb2, and Cd84 were highly enriched.
source: Focusing on myeloid genes, P2ry12, Siglech, Trem2, Cd33 and Cx3cr1 were least enriched during initial repopulation, whereas Ccl12, Cd52, Lyz2, Itgb2, and Cd84 were highly enriched (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 6D showing gene expression levels.

claim: Neutralization of CCL12 results in a significant reduction in repopulating cell numbers at 7 day recovery, but not total distance of cell spreading.
source: Here, we show that neutralization of CCL12 results in a significant reduction in repopulating cell numbers at 7 day recovery, but not total distance of cell spreading (Figure 6F–H), indicating that this chemokine may play an important role in early repopulating cell proliferation or survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 6F-H showing the effects of CCL12 neutralization.

claim: Choroid plexus myeloid cells do not repopulate until 14 days recovery, despite the appearance of myeloid cells in the adjacent brain parenchyma.
source: Here, we observe that choroid plexus myeloid cells do not repopulate until 14 days recovery, despite the appearance of myeloid cells in the adjacent brain parenchyma (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7A-B showing choroid plexus cell quantification.

claim: WM repopulating cells are CCR2/RFP-, or not a result of the infiltration of CCR2+ monocytes.
source: Utilizing Cx3cr1GFP/+/Ccr2RFP/+ mice, in which CCR2+ cells (mainly monocytes) express RFP, we show that WM repopulating cells are CCR2/RFP-, or not a result of the infiltration of CCR2+ monocytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C showing CCR2 expression analysis.

claim: 14 day PLX3397 600 ppm treatment results in an expansion, not suppression, of HSCs, common myeloid progenitors (CMPs), and granulocyte/monocyte progenitors (GMPs).
source: Here, we observe an expansion, not suppression, of HSCs, common myeloid progenitors (CMPs), and granulocyte/monocyte progenitors (GMPs) following CSF1R inhibition and/or recovery (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1F showing bone marrow cell quantification.

claim: Changes in bone marrow progenitors following 14 day PLX3397 treatment do not result in significant changes to blood or spleen myeloid cell populations.
source: However, these changes do not result in significant changes to blood or spleen myeloid cell populations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-E showing peripheral myeloid cell quantification.

claim: CX3CR1 and CCR2 KO in Cx3cr1GFP/GFP/Ccr2RFP/RFP mice elicits no alterations in WM repopulation, indicating that this form of repopulation is not dependent on these signaling axes.
source: We further explored the CCR2/CCL2 signaling axis using Ccl2-/- mice. Interestingly, we found that a lack of Ccl2 conveyed resistance to CSF1Ri-induced microglial death, with 14 day PLX3397 treatment only eliminating ~90–95% of microglia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7C-D showing repopulation in knockout mice.

claim: A lack of Ccl2 conveyed resistance to CSF1Ri-induced microglial death, with 14 day PLX3397 treatment only eliminating ~90–95% of microglia.
source: Interestingly, we found that a lack of Ccl2 conveyed resistance to CSF1Ri-induced microglial death, with 14 day PLX3397 treatment only eliminating ~90–95% of microglia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1G-H showing microglial depletion in Ccl2 KO mice.

claim: GLOBAL repopulation was observed in Ccl2-/- mice rather than WM repopulation.
source: As a result, GLOBAL repopulation was observed in these mice rather than WM repopulation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data in Ccl2 KO mice.

claim: >99% microglial elimination is a requirement for WM repopulation, which may not be achieved by 14 day PLX3397 treatment under certain conditions.
source: In combination with findings from H2K-BCL2 mice, these data confirm that >99% microglial elimination is a requirement for WM repopulation, which may not be achieved by 14 day PLX3397 treatment under certain conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data from H2K-BCL2 and Ccl2 KO mice.

claim: With head-shielded irradiation, no GFP+ cells were visible in the parenchyma of control chimeric mice, confirming that under normal conditions circulating peripheral cells do not enter the brain.
source: With HS irradiation, however, no GFP+ cells were visible in the parenchyma of control chimeric mice (Figure 7G,K), confirming that under normal conditions circulating peripheral cells do not enter the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7G,K showing absence of GFP+ cells in control chimeras.

claim: GFP+ cells were visible in the choroid plexus of control head-shielded chimera, consistent with their partial turnover by circulating BM-derived cells.
source: GFP+ cells were visible in the choroid plexus of control HS chimera (Figure 7G1), consistent with their partial turnover by circulating BM-derived cells (Kierdorf et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7G1 showing GFP+ cells in choroid plexus and a citation to a published study.

claim: Fourteen-day PLX3397 eliminated all myeloid cells in head-shielded-irradiated brains.
source: Fourteen-day PLX3397 eliminated all myeloid cells in HS-irradiated brains (Figure 7H,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7H,K showing absence of myeloid cells.

claim: By 7 day recovery, WM repopulation was apparent in head-shielded-irradiated chimeric mice, however, IBA1+ cells were GFP-, thus ruling out peripheral BM-derived cells as the source of this form of microglial repopulation.
source: By 7 day recovery, WM repopulation was apparent in HS-irradiated chimeric mice, however, IBA1+ cells were GFP- (Figure 7I–K), thus ruling out peripheral BM-derived cells as the source of this form of microglial repopulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7I-K showing lack of GFP expression in repopulating cells.

claim: At 14 day recovery in head-shielded chimeric mice, the wave of repopulating myeloid cells was visible in the cortex, as seen in WT mice.
source: At 14 day recovery, the wave of repopulating myeloid cells was visible in the cortex, as seen in WT mice (Figure 7J and J1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7J and J1 showing the repopulation wave.

claim: Since parenchymal repopulating IBA1+ cells were GFP- in head-shielded chimeric mice, these data provide strong evidence that BM-derived cells, including choroid plexus macrophages, do not contribute to WM repopulation.
source: It should be noted that since parenchymal repopulating IBA1+ cells were GFP- in HS chimeric mice, these data provide strong evidence that BM-derived cells, including choroid plexus macrophages - which are GFP+ in HS chimeric control mice - do not contribute to WM repopulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bone marrow chimera data.

claim: Surviving SVZ/WM myeloid cells serve as the major source of WM repopulation.
source: Together, these data indicate that surviving SVZ/WM myeloid cells serve as the major source of this unique form of CNS myeloid cell repopulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including lineage tracing and bone marrow chimera experiments.

claim: Control microglia show increased CD45 and CD11b in response to LPS, while repopulated cells do not change.
source: Control microglia show increased CD45 and CD11b in response to LPS, while repopulated cells do not change (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-C showing flow cytometry data.

claim: 69 DEGs were identified in WM repopulated myeloid cells compared to control microglia in the absence of LPS (logFC > 1, FDR > 0.05).
source: Unlike GLOBAL repopulation, in which control and repopulating cells display few transcriptional differences (25 DEGs in GLOBAL vs. control Figure 8—figure supplement 1F–G), we identified 69 DEGs in WM repopulated myeloid cells compared to control microglia in the absence of LPS (logFC > 1, FDR > 0.05; Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 8B showing differential gene expression analysis.

claim: GO analysis of DEGs between control and 28 day repopulated cells identified the following top five enriched pathways: regulation of cellular component size, negative regulator of chemotaxis, ameboidal-type cell migration, negative regulation of response to external stimulus, and wound healing.
source: GO analysis of DEGs between control and 28 day repopulated cells identified the following top five enriched pathways: regulation of cellular component size, negative regulator of chemotaxis, ameboidal-type cell migration, negative regulation of response to external stimulus, and wound healing (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 8C showing GO analysis results.

claim: Robust enrichment of DAM and WAM-associated genes is observed in repopulating cells, including Clec7a, Axl, Apoe, Cst7, Ctsd, and Ly9.
source: Notably, we observe robust enrichment of DAM and WAM-associated genes in repopulating cells, including Clec7a, Axl, Apoe, Cst7, Ctsd, and Ly9 (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 8D showing gene expression comparison.

claim: AXL and CLEC7A, recently identified as WAM markers, immunostaining is apparent in repopulating myeloid cells, particularly in the early stages of repopulation, and in cells located at the wavefront, whereas undetected in microglia from control brains.
source: AXL and CLEC7A, recently identified as WAM markers (Safaiyan et al., 2021), immunostaining is apparent in repopulating myeloid cells, particularly in the early stages of repopulation, and in cells located at the wavefront, whereas undetected in microglia from control brains (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 8E-F showing immunostaining and a citation to a published study.

claim: A reduction in expression of Sall1, a transcription factor unique to microglia, is observed in repopulating compared to homeostatic microglia.
source: In addition, we also observe a reduction in expression of Sall1, a transcription factor unique to microglia (Buttgereit et al., 2016), in repopulating compared to homeostatic microglia.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the gene expression data with a citation to a published study.

claim: Cluster 3 contains genes that are significantly different between control and repopulating cells across all time points, including genes implicated in clearance (Apoe, Atg2a, Axl, Wdr45b), cell growth/differentiation (Cd34, Cdk9), stress (Ier2, Ppp1r15a), inflammation (Ccrl2, H2-K2, Scimp, Tlr3), and senescence (Ubn1, Wdr45b).
source: Cluster 3 contains genes that are significantly different between control and repopulating cells across all time points, including genes implicated in clearance (Apoe, Atg2a, Axl, Wdr45b), cell growth/differentiation (Cd34, Cdk9), stress (Ier2, Ppp1r15a), inflammation (Ccrl2, H2-K2, Scimp, Tlr3), and senescence (Ubn1, Wdr45b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cluster analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Clusters 2, 5, 7, and 8 show differential responses to LPS at the 24 hr timepoint between control and repopulating cells.
source: Clusters 2 (e.g. C4b, Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, Ctsl, Ctss, Il1a, Nlrp3, Pcna, and Tnf), 5, 7 (e.g. Ccl12, Cd63, Csf1, Cxcl13, Il1b, Myc, Plek, and Nfkbib), and 8 shows differential responses to LPS at the 24 hr timepoint between control and repopulating cells (Figure 8I).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 8I showing cluster analysis results.

claim: WM repopulating cells represent a myeloid cell population that are transcriptionally and functionally distinct from adult homeostatic microglia with similarities to the recently identified subset of WAMs.
source: Together, these findings provide evidence that WM repopulating cells represent a myeloid cell population that are transcriptionally and functionally distinct from adult homeostatic microglia with similarities to the recently identified subset of WAMs, cells absent in the adult (4 months) mouse brain, but comprise 20% of microglia in the aged (24 months) mouse brain (Safaiyan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptional and functional data with a citation to a published study.

claim: 28 day recovery mice exhibit reduced locomotion.
source: Here, we performed a battery of cognitive and behavior tasks in 28 day recovery mice (Figure 9A–H) and observe that these mice exhibit reduced locomotion (Figure 9A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 9A-B showing behavioral data.

claim: 28 day recovery mice exhibit reduced ability to discriminate a novel place change compared to controls.
source: and reduced ability to discriminate a novel place change compared to controls (Figure 9H).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 9H showing behavioral data.

claim: 28 day recovery mice do not exhibit overt cognitive, behavioral, or health changes.
source: However, we observe no other significant behavior or cognitive disruptions. Overall, these animals do not appear to exhibit overt cognitive, behavioral, or health changes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the behavioral testing results.

claim: Cx3cr1-GFP+ repopulating myeloid cells react to a focal laser injury with similar rates of migration as homeostatic microglia.
source: Cx3cr1-GFP+ repopulating myeloid cells react to a focal laser injury with similar rates of migration as homeostatic microglia (Figure 9J, Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 9J and Videos 1 and 2 showing live imaging data.

claim: Extension and retraction of processes (i.e. motility) were similar between control microglia and repopulating cells, although repopulating cells displayed fewer and thicker processes.
source: Furthermore, extension and retraction of processes (i.e. motility) were similar between control microglia and repopulating cells, although repopulating cells displayed fewer and thicker processes as previously demonstrated (Figure 9K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 9K-L showing motility measurements.

claim: Fourteen-day treatment of high-dose PLX3397 results in significant elevation in PNN staining.
source: Fourteen-day treatment of high-dose PLX3397 results in significant elevation in PNN staining, corroborating previous findings that microglia play a critical homeostatic role in modulating these structures (Crapser et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing increased PNN staining and a citation to a published study.

claim: Following CSF1Ri withdrawal and subsequent 28 day recovery, PNN staining returns to normal levels, indicating that WM repopulating cells share similar PNN-regulating capacities as homeostatic microglia.
source: Following CSF1Ri withdrawal and subsequent 28 day recovery, PNN staining returns to normal levels (Figure 9M–N), indicating that WM repopulating cells share similar PNN-regulating capacities as homeostatic microglia.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 9M-N showing PNN staining quantification.

claim: In early postnatal development, a population of amoeboid microglia migrating from the ventricular zone into the corpus callosum phagocytose oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) prior to myelination.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that WM and developing microglia contribute to myelinogenesis/oligodendrocyte progenitor maintenance (Marsters et al., 2020; Hagemeyer et al., 2017). In early postnatal development, a population of amoeboid microglia migrating from the ventricular zone into the corpus callosum phagocytose oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) prior to myelination (Nemes-Baran et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: In 28 day recovery mice, no changes are observed in Olig2, a marker for cells of oligodendrocyte lineage.
source: However, unlike during development in which these cells participate in oligo/myelinogenesis, in 28 day recovery mice we observe no changes in Olig2, a marker for cells of oligodendrocyte lineage (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,D showing Olig2 staining.

claim: In 28 day recovery mice, no changes are observed in PDGFRα, a marker for oligodendrocyte progenitor cells.
source: or PDGFRα, a marker for oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 1B,E showing PDGFRα staining.

claim: Although not statistically significant there appears to be a slight decrease in MBP staining in 28 day recovery mice, indicating that these cells could be involved in MBP clearance.
source: Although not statistically significant there appears to be a slight decrease in MBP staining, indicating that these cells could be involved in MBP clearance.
evidence: This is an observation from the MBP staining data with speculative interpretation.

claim: WM repopulating cells maintain reduced cell density after 3 months recovery.
source: Morphological analysis of IBA1+ cells shows that WM repopulating cells maintain reduced cell density (Figure 10C)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 10C showing cell quantification.

claim: WM repopulating cells maintain amoeboid-like cell characteristics after 3 months recovery, including larger cell body size, reduced number of processes, and reduced process length.
source: and amoeboid-like cell characteristics, including larger cell body size (Figure 10D), reduced number of processes (Figure 10E), and reduced process length (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 10D-F showing morphological measurements.

claim: Transcriptional differences remain in the brain three months following CSF1Ri withdrawal.
source: Bulk tissue RNAseq analysis (Figure 10H) highlights that transcriptional differences remain in the brain three mo following CSF1Ri withdrawal (Figure 10I).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 10H-I showing gene expression analysis.

claim: Similar to earlier WM repopulation timepoints, DEG analysis at 3 months recovery highlights a downregulation in homeostatic-associated microglial gene P2ry12 and upregulation in DAM/WAM-associated genes Clec7a.
source: Similar to earlier WM repopulation timepoints, DEG analysis highlights a downregulation in homeostatic-associated microglial gene P2ry12 and upregulation in DAM/WAM-associated genes Clec7a (Figure 10I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 10I-J showing gene expression analysis.

claim: GO term analysis of 3 month recovery shows that upregulated DEGs are involved in neuron projection development, axon guidance, synaptic transmission, and synaptic potential, providing evidence that WM repopulating cells could play an important role in axonal homeostasis.
source: GO term analysis shows that upregulated DEGs are involved in neuron projection development, axon guidance, synaptic transmission, and synaptic potential, providing evidence that WM repopulating cells could play an important role in axonal homeostasis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GO term analysis results.

claim: WM repopulating microglia represent a distinct population of myeloid cells rather than a slower restoration of the microglial phenotype.
source: Together, these data show that WM repopulating microglia represent a distinct population of myeloid cells rather than a slower restoration of the microglial phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the long-term morphological and transcriptional data.
